column3: Near-verbatim continuation: people dispute about God without knowledge, adding the absence of guidance and illuminating scripture.
The story shows Satan attaching to one who abandoned signs, an inverse but relevant picture of satanic pursuit and misguidance.
Satanic temptation is relevant, but neither uninformed disputation nor following is stated.
It pairs being without knowledge with leading people away from God's path, closely reinforcing the focus's epistemic failure.
The immediate continuation specifies that whoever takes the rebellious devil as patron is led astray and toward the Blaze.
It identifies disputation concerning God's signs with disbelief, though it does not explicitly repeat the lack of knowledge.
A near-parallel repeats disputing about God without knowledge and adds the lack of guidance and scripture.
Those who dispute about God's signs are shown to have no escape, supplying the consequence without the focus's twofold formulation.
It denies a satanic source for revelation, a limited contrast to following devils.
The verse explicitly names every rebellious devil, but frames exclusion from heaven rather than human following.
The same local figure misleads from God's path and receives disgrace in this world and burning punishment at resurrection.
It calls Satan an enemy who summons his party to the Blaze, clarifying the danger of following him.
It condemns disputing about God's signs without authority, a close evidentiary counterpart to disputing without knowledge.
It explicitly prohibits following Satan's steps and explains their corrupting direction.
It contrasts following revelation with following other protectors, supplying the normative alternative to the focus.
It directly joins following desire without knowledge to misguidance and absence of helpers.
A nearby description of unstable devotion ends in loss in this world and the Hereafter, extending the local misdirection theme.
It commands following the messenger for guidance, only a positive contrast to the focus.
It identifies devils as excluded hostile agents, but does not address people following them.
Following Pharaoh's unsound command gives a comparable pattern of following an unfit leader.
Entrenched rebellion and punishment resonate with the focus's rebellious-devil element, without the act of following.
It explicitly diagnoses following desire without divine guidance as the deepest misguidance.
The local verse concerns an attempted scheme and divine support, not uninformed dispute or satanic following.
Persistent disputation shows argument becoming resistant excess, though its object and epistemic condition differ.
It rejects Satan as the source of the Qur'an, a useful source-level contrast to satanic allegiance.
Pharaoh leads his people into the Fire, extending the pattern of disastrous following and its outcome.
Following the Prophet by believers is a broad positive counterpart only.
Fabricating lies about God without knowledge to mislead people closely matches the focus's uninformed speech about God.
The believers' reluctance at departure does not develop the focus's dispute or satanic-following themes.
The immediate later passage addresses being disputed with, but shifts to God's knowledge of deeds rather than the focus's diagnosis.
Opposing the messenger and following a way other than believers leads to Hell, a consequential parallel for wrong following.
It portrays disputing after truth has become clear, an adjacent form of resistant argument.
Satanic incitement and seeking refuge in God illuminate resistance to satanic pressure.
It explicitly identifies the invoked object as a rebellious devil, exactly matching the focus's designation.
It commands following the revealed way and not the desires of those who do not know, a strong corrective counterpart.
Following a means in travel does not bear on moral or epistemic following.
It asks who can dispute with God on another's behalf at the final judgment, extending the gravity of disputing before God.
Taking desire as a god and being led astray shows a related rejection of sound guidance, though it says on knowledge.
Becoming Satan's ally through punishment gives a related allegiance outcome without the focus's stated action.
The verse lists devils subject to Solomon and supplies little interpretive leverage for the focus.
The messenger's following of revelation is only a general positive contrast.
Disputing for oneself at final recompense is distinct from disputing about God without knowledge.
The resurrection proof in the local sequence does not directly clarify the focus's two actions.
The confirming Arabic scripture and its warning do not materially develop the focus.
Satan abandoning a person after turning him from remembrance is a limited related consequence.
Following Abraham is a positive affiliation context rather than a parallel to wrongful following.
Rejecting revelation as an ancient lie shows opposition, but not the focus's argument or satanic following.
It names Satan as a clear enemy who blocks the path, explaining why his direction must not be followed.
Moses requests to follow in order to learn right guidance, a remote positive counterexample.
Calling clear truth manifest magic is a related rejection, but it does not develop the focus's formulation.
Following divine guidance is a broad positive alternative to the focus's wrong following.
The account of Solomon and the queen does not materially connect to the focus.
Seeking refuge from satanic promptings supports resistance to the satanic influence named in the focus.
It singles out those most intense in rebellion for judgment, resonating with the rebellious-devil description.
Those disputing God's signs are diverted from the right course, though lack of knowledge is not restated.
The list of righteous figures has no material connection to the focus.
Devils are prepared for the Blaze, supplying a limited consequence for the agents the focus says are followed.
The prohibition on pursuing what one has no knowledge of directly reinforces the focus's epistemic condition.
Following inherited practice despite its lack of understanding and guidance parallels unexamined following.
The list of patient figures has no material connection to the focus.
Satan's beautification of deeds explains a mechanism by which people persist in a misguided course.
A person whose speech invokes God while being fiercely contentious gives a related portrayal of destructive disputation.
Devils driving disbelievers onward shows their active misdirecting role.
Lying about God or denying truth is paired with Hell, a close consequence-level parallel to wrongful speech about God.
It warns against following desires after knowledge has come, a strong inverse to the focus's following without knowledge.
The painful punishment of rejecters is relevant only at the broad consequence level.
It calls certain practices Satan's work and commands avoidance, but does not concern following or disputation.
The poets wandering in every valley does not materially clarify the focus.
It explicitly condemns disputing God's signs without authority and commands refuge in God from its arrogant drive.
The verse concerns wavering under persecution rather than the focus's dispute or satanic following.
The severing of ties between followers and followed under punishment clarifies the failure of wrongful allegiance.
It directly prohibits following Satan's steps because he is a clear enemy.
Turning from the Merciful's remembrance is answered by an accompanying Satan, showing a pathway into satanic attachment.
It identifies the human being as especially given to disputation, offering a broad characterization of the focus's conduct.
The lawful marital dispute heard by God is a distinct, constructive use of disputation.
Leading others astray without knowledge shares the focus's epistemic fault and adds shared burden at judgment.
Human and jinn devils exchange deceptive speech, supplying a wider setting for satanic misleading.
False partners, embellished plotting, and being barred from the path are only a general related context.
Successive generations do not involve the focus's moral sense of following.
Speaking abusively about God without knowledge is an adjacent but different form of uninformed speech.
Following conjecture cannot replace truth, directly exposing the insufficiency of a knowledge-less basis for following.
Universal praise and divine knowledge do not materially connect to the focus.
The opponents' claim that followers obey an enchanted man is a remote example of accusatory rhetoric.
The divine title alone does not develop the focus.
Satan's domination makes people forget God and forms his party, clarifying the effect of satanic allegiance.
Unintentional harm without knowledge in a treaty setting is unrelated to the focus's epistemic blame.
It warns that following others' desires after knowledge leads to wrongdoing, a strong counterpart to the focus's misdirected following.
It commands judgment by revelation and forbids following desires that would turn one from what God revealed.
It warns against following desires after knowledge has come and names the loss of divine protector or guard.
It explicitly says people followed what devils recited and contrasts harmful learning with real knowledge.
The sound heart at God's meeting does not materially develop the focus.
It contrasts following falsehood with following truth, supplying the central moral distinction behind the focus's following.
Satan is explicitly a clear enemy of humankind, reinforcing the agent the focus says is followed.
The false accusation that listeners follow an enchanted man is only a remote rhetorical parallel.
Pilgrimage regulations do not materially connect to the focus.
Following what angers God results in voided deeds, a consequential parallel for wrongful following.
The condemned blame earlier communities for leading them astray in the Fire, a broad outcome of misdirected following.
It explicitly makes Hell the full recompense for those who follow Satan.
The trumpet blast alone does not clarify the focus.
Following the messengers is a general positive counterexample to following devils.
It explicitly commands entering fully into submission and forbids following Satan's steps because he is a clear enemy.
Satan declares that he will lead people astray and command them, directly describing his misdirecting agency.
Satan's promises and wishful thinking show the deceptive mechanism behind allegiance to him.
Abraham's people dispute with him concerning God, furnishing a direct but differently framed instance of disputation about God.
Devils inspire their allies to dispute with believers, directly joining satanic influence to contentious speech.
It expressly forbids following Satan's steps, a direct counterpart to the focus's following of every rebellious devil.
It forbids following the desires of those who deny God's signs, a related form of unguided allegiance.
Satan declares his intent to sit on God's straight path and divert people from it, clarifying the directional opposition behind the focus.
Satan's deception of the first pair supplies a foundational instance of his misleading activity.
A satanic provocation is met with seeking refuge in God, providing the opposing response to satanic pressure.
God-conscious people remember when touched by Satan and regain clear sight, contrasting with continuing to follow him.
The one who followed his desire after receiving signs gives a close narrative analogue to abandoning guidance for a corrupt directing force.
Devils made past communities' deeds attractive, explaining how misguided conduct becomes compelling.
The command to seek refuge from the expelled Satan gives the appropriate counter-movement to satanic following.
Satan seeks to sow discord among people, connecting destructive speech with satanic intervention.
Satan is authorized to draw people by voice, incite them, and share in their pursuits, a detailed picture of his recruiting power.
It condemns taking Satan and his progeny as protectors besides God, directly opposing the allegiance described in the focus.
It prohibits obeying one who follows desire after neglecting God's remembrance, a close wrongful-following parallel.
Abraham forbids worshipping Satan and identifies him as disobedient to the Merciful, directly illuminating the focus's rebellious devil.
Satan whispers to Adam, an early instance of his deceptive guidance.
It states that truth cannot follow people's desires, sharply contrasting truth with desire-led direction.
Taking one's desire as a god gives a strong analogue to submitting one's direction to a false authority.
God's covenant with the children of Adam explicitly forbids worshipping Satan because he is a clear enemy.
David is forbidden to follow desire because it diverts from God's way, closely pairing wrongful following with loss of the path.
It contrasts one who follows clear proof from God with one who follows evil desire, directly clarifying the focus's competing directions.
It condemns following conjecture and desire despite guidance having come, a close epistemic counterpart to following without knowledge.
Satan commands disbelief and then disowns his follower, clarifying the treachery of satanic allegiance.
The verse explicitly says people dispute concerning God while affirming His overwhelming power.
The ruler's argument with Abraham about his Lord is a direct but narrative-specific instance of disputation about God.
Disbelievers dispute by falsehood in order to refute truth, identifying a corrupt use of argument closely related to the focus.
